requirement:
After preparation and selection discovery succeed, and before any selected
test starts, Habeas atomically establishes the new coverage set:

- An unfiltered workspace invocation clears the entire previous set,
  including results for tests that no longer exist. This includes
  `habeas coverage` with no supplied arguments and `habeas test`.
- An invocation with an explicit package or binary restriction, test filter,
  partition, or ignored-only selection is filtered. It clears results for all
  selected test identities and preserves unselected results within the
  active build configuration.
- Every selected test receives a pending entry without measurements.

Native default filters and the default handling of ignored tests still apply
to an unfiltered workspace invocation. `--run-ignored all` alone does not make
a workspace invocation filtered.

A selected test that never starts because of fail-fast, interruption, or
execution startup failure remains unavailable. Its previous result does not
become available again. A filtered selection containing no tests leaves the
current results and active configuration unchanged; an empty unfiltered
workspace selection clears the previous set.

If the atomic replacement cannot be committed, the command reports the
failure and starts no tests. The previously committed coverage set and active
configuration remain unchanged.
rationale: Add a test, marked with {test}`requirements.test-coverage.storage.replace`, for an unfiltered workspace invocation whose selection is narrowed only by native defaults. First produce saved results for tests that the native defaults will exclude. Examples are a test excluded by a nextest `default-filter` and an `#[ignore]` test. Then run `habeas coverage` with no arguments, or with only `--workspace --run-ignored all`. Assert that the new selection holds only the default-selected tests, that the results for the default-excluded tests are cleared, and that they are not preserved as they would be in a filtered run. — The text requires that native default filters and default ignored-test handling still apply to an unfiltered workspace invocation. It also says `--run-ignored all` alone does not make an invocation filtered. The supplied tests cover only the argument classification, in `src/execution_coverage/runner.rs#mod[tests]/fn[explicit_filters_are_distinguished_from_workspace_run_settings]`. That test calls `filtered(...)` on argument lists and never touches stored results. In `tests/execution_coverage.rs`, `default_coverage_and_test_replace_removed_tests` has no default filter or ignored tests configured. `configured_retries_filters_profiles_and_libtest_arguments_are_preserved` sets `default-filter`, but it is not marked for this requirement and starts with no earlier results. The `habeas test` path in `full_test_flow_checks_real_function_counters_after_all_tests` also has no earlier results. In `package_binary_partition_and_ignored_selection_replace_only_their_actual_test_identities`, the ignored-test result is only preserved by filtered reruns. Nothing runs an unfiltered invocation over earlier results and shows that tests excluded by a default filter or default ignore handling are cleared. A faulty implementation could treat a run narrowed by default filters as filtered, because it selects fewer tests than the whole set. That implementation would leave stale results for the excluded tests, and every reviewed test would still pass.

output.rationale:
`requirements.test-coverage.storage.replace` has no implementation roots, and I found no structural obligation that needs implementation evidence. I read the requirement text and checked that it has no Implements edges.

Every clause specifies observable behavior:
- Unfiltered invocations clear the whole previous set. Filtered invocations clear only the selected identities and preserve the rest.
- Every selected test gets a pending entry.
- Selected tests that never start stay unavailable.
- An empty filtered selection changes nothing.
- A failed commit reports the failure, starts no tests, and leaves the prior set and active configuration unchanged.

I considered "atomically establishes the new coverage set" as a candidate structural obligation. It names no library, algorithm, type, signature, or interface. An implementation could use a database transaction, write a temporary file and rename it, or swap an in-memory snapshot. Each of these produces the same results, because the previous state is kept on failure and the new state appears all at once. The text prescribes none of them, so the mechanism is discretionary and tests can verify the behavior.

The ordering clause, "After preparation and selection discovery succeed, and before any selected test starts", is also observable behavior, since it fixes when the replacement happens relative to test starts. It does not require any particular code structure.

So no root needs an {impl} reference, and I found no gap.
